props.title: Backup Plan

sections.content: The Back-up Plan (2010) - not 2012 - falls into the well-worn territory of romantic comedies about pregnancy and unconventional families, following similar beats to Knocked Up (2007) and Baby Mama (2008). Jennifer Lopez plays a single woman who gets artificially inseminated, only to meet her perfect match immediately after. The film represents a specific moment in rom-com history when Hollywood was trying to modernize traditional family narratives while still clinging to conventional happy endings. It shares DNA with The Switch (2010) and Life as We Know It (2010), all exploring how modern reproductive choices intersect with romance.

sections.content: The film sits at an interesting intersection of medical rom-coms like Junior (1994) and more serious explorations of modern parenthood like Juno (2007). While Lopez brings her trademark charm, the script relies heavily on pregnancy slapstick and sitcom-style misunderstandings that were already feeling dated by 2010. The film's attempts to address serious topics about single motherhood by choice get undermined by its need to fulfill romantic comedy conventions. SUBHEAD: Evolution of Pregnancy in Romance Films

Looking at how pregnancy narratives evolved in romantic films, we see a clear progression from Look Who's Talking (1989) through Knocked Up (2007) to more nuanced modern takes like Obvious Child (2014). The Back-up Plan tries to bridge traditional rom-com formulas with contemporary reproductive choices, but struggles to fully commit to either approach. This tension reflects Hollywood's broader challenge in updating romantic comedy tropes for modern audiences.
